title: “The Dreamer?” The Aleatoric Prelude and Fugue No.3, Book I
content_blocks: Another thing that I learned from Lutosławski (along with New York avant garde composers Earle Brown, Morton Feldman, and others) as a young composer was the use of chance in music. In this prelude and fugue, the idea of chance (or ‘aleatory,’ coming from the Latin ‘alea’, meaning dice) applies to rhythm and time. I wrote out only approximate rhythms and durations. Trills and repeated figures, for instance, can be played for longer and shorter times, as the performer decides. The music can play out aggressively or languidly, very rhythmically or without any sense of time.

The prelude is marked by trills that start slowly and accelerate, against which are played repeated leaping figures.  Despite the unusual structure of the mode—it’s the same as that used in Prelude and Fugue No.10, mentioned in my “Birdsong!” post—the note D is clearly the center of the piece.

The fugue subject has a clear shape, but ever-changing intervals (again, an example of the diatonic answers I described earlier). What makes this fugue especially unusual—over and above the flexibility of the rhythm and tempo—is that the fugue subject enters at unpredictable times, often overlapping with one note or another of the previous entry of the subject. It’s not that these later entries are being “impolite,” but more like they’re not quite paying careful attention. They’re dreamers—the subtitle I gave this pair—off in their own world! Curiously, despite that this is a four-voice fugue, I always get a feeling of loneliness in this music. Are dreamers lonely? Or just oblivious?

Notwithstanding those unusual features of this fugue, the characters of the subject and both the first and second countersubject are maintained throughout the fugue (in a manner more typical of a triple fugue):  the subject is forlorn and sustained, the first countersubject focuses on oscillations (continued from the Prelude), while the second countersubject is like a mournful repeated two-note bird-song.
You can listen to Steve Beck’s insightful performance of the Prelude and Fugue online.
